quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on what huckaback and mock leno are, how they are built and what they are used for.

questions.q: What is the essential structure of a huckaback?
options: A warp-faced satin with a long float
Two layers of plain weave stitched together
Ends crossed over each other by a doup heald
Blocks of plain weave alternating with blocks of short floats
questions.explain: Huckaback alternates plain-weave blocks with blocks where ends and picks float over three or more threads. The other options describe satin, double cloth and true leno.

questions.q: Why is huckaback used for towels and glass cloths?
options: Its floats stand out from the plain ground and make a rough, absorbent surface
It is the strongest of all weaves
It is completely smooth and lint-free
questions.explain: The floats give a rough surface that holds water, which is what a towel needs; smoothness and lustre are not the aim.

questions.q: Over how many threads do the floats of a huckaback pass, according to the lecture?
questions.explain: The lecture says ends (and picks) float over three or more threads in the float blocks; a float over one thread is just plain weave.

questions.q: What does a true leno do that a mock leno does not?
options: Crosses the ends over each other with a doup heald
questions.explain: A true leno physically crosses the ends with a doup heald; a mock leno only imitates the open look on an ordinary dobby by grouping threads.

questions.q: A mock leno needs a special doup heald to be woven.
questions.explain: The whole point of a mock leno is that it is woven with ordinary healds on a dobby; the doup is needed only for true leno.

questions.q: How does a mock leno produce its perforated appearance?
options: Ends and picks are grouped so they crowd together in some places and leave gaps in others
The weft is cut away after weaving
Alternate ends are left out of the reed
questions.explain: Grouping of floats and plain interlacings makes threads bunch together and leave open spaces, which reads as a gauze-like perforation.

questions.q: How many healds does the lecture's Huckaback 1 (10 ends × 6 picks) require?
questions.explain: The draft shown uses four healds with the threading order 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3.

questions.q: Huckaback 2 in the lecture has a square repeat of 10 ends by 10 picks.
questions.explain: Huckaback 2 is given as 10 ends × 10 picks, whereas Huckaback 1 is 10 ends × 6 picks.

questions.q: Which of the lecture's examples has a square repeat of 12 ends × 12 picks?
questions.explain: Only Mock leno A is 12 × 12; B is 8 × 8, C is 14 × 14, D is 16 × 16, and Huckaback 2 is 10 × 10.

questions.q: The lecture describes both huckaback and mock leno as open, absorbent weaves.
questions.explain: The subtitle groups them as open, absorbent weaves: huckaback for towels and mock leno imitating the gauze of a true leno.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How repeat size, draft and float length relate in huckaback and mock leno structures.

questions.q: A weave repeats on 10 ends and is threaded 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3. What does the number of healds equal?
options: The number of different heald numbers used: 4
questions.explain: The heald count is the number of distinct heald numbers in the threading, here 1, 2, 3 and 4 — four healds. Ends that interlace alike share a heald.

questions.q: If the float length in a huckaback's float blocks is increased, what happens to the surface?
options: Identical, since floats do not affect feel
Rougher and more absorbent but weaker, with floats more liable to snag
questions.explain: Longer floats stand further from the ground and hold more water, but they are less firmly bound and snag more easily.

questions.q: Which relationship fixes the number of repeats of a 10-end huckaback across a warp?
questions.explain: Repeats across the width = total ends ÷ ends per repeat. Multiplying would give an absurd number.

questions.q: In a lifting plan for Huckaback 1, the number of rows equals the number of picks in the repeat, six.
questions.explain: A peg plan has one row per pick of the repeat and one column per heald, so Huckaback 1 needs 6 rows × 4 columns.

questions.q: A mock leno groups its threads. What happens to the thread spacing as the grouping is made stronger (longer floats on the group edges)?
options: The gaps between groups become larger and the cloth more open
The cloth becomes denser and closed
Nothing changes until a doup is added
questions.explain: Stronger grouping pulls threads closer together inside each group and widens the open spaces between groups.

questions.q: Huckaback 1 repeats on 10 ends × 6 picks. How many squares does one repeat occupy on point paper?
questions.explain: Squares = ends × picks = 10 × 6 = 60. Adding 10 + 6 = 16 is the usual slip.

questions.q: Two ends threaded on the same heald in a huckaback must…
options: lift on exactly the same picks
be in the same reed dent
questions.explain: A heald lifts all its ends together, so ends on one heald interlace identically; the draft groups ends by their lifting pattern.

questions.q: Changing a huckaback from 10 × 6 to 10 × 10 changes the number of healds required.
questions.explain: Healds depend on the number of differently interlacing ends, not on picks; the number of picks only changes the length of the peg plan.

questions.q: In a mock leno D of 16 ends × 16 picks woven at 48 ends per inch, how is the repeat width in the cloth found?
questions.explain: Width = ends in repeat ÷ ends per inch = 16 ÷ 48 = 0.333 inch; the reciprocal gives repeats per inch, not width.

questions.q: A huckaback is woven from the same yarn at a lower sett. Which effect follows?
options: More open and absorbent, but floats less supported
questions.explain: Lower sett opens the structure, which helps absorbency but leaves the floats with fewer neighbours to hold them in place.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Counting ends, healds, repeats and floats for the huckaback and mock leno examples.

questions.q: Huckaback 1 is threaded 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3. How many ends of the 10-end repeat are drawn on heald 1?
questions.explain: Heald 1 appears at positions 1, 3 and 5 of the threading: three ends. Healds 2 and 4 carry two ends each, healds 1 and 3 three each.

questions.q: Using the same threading 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3, how many ends in one repeat are on heald 4?
questions.explain: Heald 4 appears at positions 7 and 9 only, so two ends per repeat.

questions.q: A huckaback towel warp has 2,400 ends. The weave repeats on 10 ends. How many complete repeats are there across the warp?
questions.explain: 2,400 ÷ 10 = 240 repeats of the 10-end weave.

questions.q: Huckaback 1 (10 ends × 6 picks) is woven at 50 picks per inch. How many repeats are woven in one inch of cloth length? Give two decimals.
questions.explain: Repeats per inch lengthwise = picks per inch ÷ picks per repeat = 50 ÷ 6 = 8.33.

questions.q: A huckaback towel loom runs at 180 picks per minute at 90 % efficiency. With Huckaback 2 (10 picks per repeat) how many repeats are woven per minute?
questions.explain: Picks actually inserted = 180 × 0.9 = 162 per minute; 162 ÷ 10 picks per repeat = 16.2 repeats.

questions.q: Mock leno C repeats on 14 ends × 14 picks. How many point-paper squares does one repeat contain?
questions.explain: 14 × 14 = 196 squares.

questions.q: A warp of 3,360 ends is to be woven in Mock leno D (16-end repeat). How many ends are left over after the last complete repeat?
questions.explain: 3,360 ÷ 16 = 210 exactly, so no ends are left over; the warp fits the repeat perfectly.

questions.q: Mock leno A (12 ends per repeat) is set at 60 ends per inch. How many repeats are there per inch of width?
questions.explain: 60 ÷ 12 = 5 repeats per inch across the width.

questions.q: On point paper a huckaback end is shown lifted on picks 1, 2 and 3 and down on picks 4, 5 and 6 of a 6-pick repeat. What is its longest float?
questions.explain: The end floats over picks 1–3 (a 3-pick warp float) and under picks 4–6 (a 3-pick weft float); the longest float is 3.

questions.q: Huckaback 1 needs 4 healds for 10 ends; Huckaback 2 needs the same threading. A loom has 8 healds. How many separate huckaback drafts of this kind could be threaded side by side?
questions.explain: 8 healds ÷ 4 healds per draft = 2 drafts. Dividing by ends instead of healds is the common error.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Mill and design-room scenarios: choosing between huckaback, mock leno and true leno, and fixing faults.

questions.q: A buyer wants an absorbent kitchen towel with a rough surface. Which weave from the lecture would you offer?
questions.explain: Huckaback's floats on a plain ground give exactly the rough, absorbent surface wanted in towels and glass cloths.

questions.q: A customer wants the open, gauze-like look of leno but your mill has only plain dobby looms without doup healds. What do you propose?
options: A mock leno, which imitates the perforated look with ordinary healds
questions.explain: Mock leno is designed for exactly this: it groups ends and picks on an ordinary dobby to imitate true leno gauze.

questions.q: A huckaback towel comes back with loose threads pulled out of the surface after washing. What is the most likely cause?
options: Floats too long or the sett too open, so the floats snagged
questions.explain: Long or poorly supported floats snag; shortening them or firming the sett cures it. The threading and repeat size are not faults.

questions.q: A sample of mock leno shows an even, closed surface with no visible gaps. What has probably gone wrong?
options: The sett is too high, so the grouped threads cannot separate to leave gaps
questions.explain: Mock leno depends on threads being free to crowd together and leave spaces; a sett that is too dense fills the gaps.

questions.q: The design office must weave Huckaback 1 on a loom fitted with only two healds. What is the problem?
options: The draft needs four healds, so the loom cannot weave it
The loom will weave it as a mock leno instead
questions.explain: The threading 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3 uses four distinct healds; two healds can weave only plain weave.

questions.q: For a glass cloth that must leave no lint, the long floats of a huckaback are a disadvantage and a plainer, shorter-float version is preferable.
questions.explain: Longer floats shed more fibre and snag; glass cloths use a firmer huckaback with short floats.

questions.q: Which production change shortens the lifting plan a weaver must peg for a mock leno?
options: Choosing Mock leno B (8 picks) instead of D (16 picks)
questions.explain: The peg plan has one row per pick of the repeat, so an 8-pick repeat needs half the rows of a 16-pick one.

questions.q: A towel manufacturer wants more absorbency from the same yarn and sett. Which huckaback change is most effective?
options: Replace the float blocks with plain weave
Reduce the picks per inch to zero
Lengthen the floats in the float blocks
questions.explain: The floats are what hold water; lengthening them increases absorbency, within the limit of snagging.

questions.q: A mock leno curtain fabric is to be woven at 60 ends per inch. Which repeat gives whole repeats across a 48-inch warp with no odd ends?
questions.explain: Total ends = 48 × 60 = 2,880; 2,880 ÷ 12 = 240 exactly, while 2,880 ÷ 14 = 205.7 leaves part of a repeat.

questions.q: Because a mock leno is woven on ordinary healds, its ends do not cross over each other in the cloth.
questions.explain: Only a true leno with a doup heald crosses the ends; a mock leno keeps the ends parallel and relies on grouping for its open effect.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder questions mixing drafts, repeats and the differences between huckaback, mock leno and true leno.

questions.q: A huckaback warp has 2,400 ends threaded 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3 repeatedly. How many ends are on heald 1 in the whole warp?
questions.explain: 240 repeats × 3 ends per repeat on heald 1 = 720 ends.

questions.q: In the same warp (2,400 ends, threading 1 2 1 2 1 3 4 3 4 3), how many ends are on heald 2?
questions.explain: 240 repeats × 2 ends per repeat on heald 2 = 480 ends.

questions.q: Huckaback 1 repeats on 10 ends × 6 picks. Which statement about weaving it is correct?
options: The peg plan has 6 rows and 4 columns
The peg plan has 10 rows and 6 columns
It cannot be woven on a dobby
questions.explain: Rows = picks in the repeat (6); columns = healds (4). A 10-row plan would be for Huckaback 2 (10 picks).

questions.q: Which is the correct contrast between huckaback and mock leno?
options: Mock leno is for towels; huckaback for curtains
Huckaback has no floats; mock leno has long floats
Huckaback relies on floats on a plain ground for texture; mock leno relies on grouping to leave gaps
Huckaback needs a doup; mock leno does not
questions.explain: Huckaback's floats make a rough absorbent surface; mock leno groups threads to open perforations. Neither uses a doup.

questions.q: A mock leno D (16 × 16) is woven at 64 ends and 64 picks per inch. How many repeats are there in one square inch of cloth?
questions.explain: 4 repeats across × 4 repeats up = 16 repeats per square inch.

questions.q: If an end in Huckaback 1 floats over three picks, the weft picks it floats over must each be floating under it, so the cloth is weak at that spot.
questions.explain: A warp float over three picks is still bound by the neighbouring ends that interlace with those picks; the cloth is only locally less firm, and the floats are deliberate.

questions.q: A designer draws Huckaback 1 but by mistake threads it 1 2 1 2 1 1 2 1 2 1. What follows?
options: Only two healds are used, so the two halves of the repeat weave alike and the huckaback effect is lost
The cloth becomes a true leno
questions.explain: Huckaback needs the two halves of the repeat to interlace differently; putting both halves on healds 1 and 2 removes that difference.

questions.q: A towel loom weaves Huckaback 2 (10 picks per repeat) at 54 picks per inch. How long is one repeat in the cloth, in inches? Give three decimals.
questions.explain: Length of a repeat = picks per repeat ÷ picks per inch = 10 ÷ 54 = 0.185 inch.

questions.q: Which lecture example has the largest repeat on point paper?
questions.explain: 16 × 16 = 256 squares, more than 196, 144 or 100.

questions.q: A true leno and a mock leno give exactly the same open look and the same stability because both leave gaps between groups of threads.
questions.explain: Only the true leno locks the gaps by crossing the ends; in a mock leno the threads can slip, so the two are not equal in stability.
